title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 9: GMA's Legacy in Education
keywords: proposal for a permanent CHEd chair
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's June 22, 2008 Inquirer column urging President Arroyo to make education 'one of her enduring legacies,' built on his own family's faith that education is 'the gateway to success and the way out of grinding poverty'

His autobiographical proof -- a father who 'valued education' and pushed all four children through college, his own FEU scholarship sustained by selling bibles and hawking newspapers, and the graduate degrees he later gave his children and even his law clerks

His indictment of the government's 'sheer neglect of higher education' -- the failure to meet 'the 12-year global standard,' the call for a qualified, permanent CHEd chair, and the ignored recommendations of the January 2008 Education Summit

His appeal that, like the self-made Diosdado Macapagal, GMA prioritize 'academic excellence' -- appointing a permanent CHEd chair and organizing the Legal Education Board -- to leave 'a legacy in education' that frees Filipinos from 'ignorance and poverty'
sub_topics: The family creed: CJP's father 'did not finish high school' (his mother 'hardly attended primary school'), yet 'valued education as the gateway to success and the way out of grinding poverty,' working 'doubly hard as a lowly government employee' to send all four children through college -- sister Tessie graduating 'summa cum laude,' brother Nardo topping 'the board exam for electrical engineers,' and Ate Loleng finishing commerce

The FEU scholarship: his father, whose 'impossible dream' was a law career, overruled CJP's wish for chemical engineering and steered him to law -- but, unable to 'afford the bus fare' to UP, was told 'Diyan ka sa FEU. Hindi na kailangan ang pamasahe,' advice made 'prophetic' when his father died during CJP's pre-law freshman year

Working through school: with his elder siblings providing 'shelter and meals,' CJP kept his FEU scholarship and earned pocket money by 'selling bibles to [his] professors and textbooks to [his] classmates,' having earlier 'hawked newspapers, peddled cigarettes, and shined shoes' in his school days

Passing on the aspiration: unable to pursue a Yale master's 'due to lack of means,' he 'visited on [his] children [his] frustrated postgraduate aspiration' -- his four daughters earning graduate degrees at the Universities of California, Chicago, Michigan and Harvard, and his son Archie earning 'two masters and a PhD' at Stanford -- and helped his law clerks win scholarships at Harvard, Columbia, University College London and Toronto

The purpose of the 'breast-thumping': begging pardon for the 'immodest breast-thumping,' CJP says he meant only to show that 'in a poor country... the ultimate aspiration of parents is to have their children... educated,' and 'to urge President Macapagal-Arroyo to prioritize education'

The neglect of higher education: readers had 'bewailed' the failure to meet 'the 12-year global standard in basic education and its sheer neglect of higher education' -- illustrated by the 170-member PACU's call for a 'permanent head' of CHEd, its president Gonzalo Duque faulting acting chair Romulo Neri (whose 'brilliance is misplaced' and who, lacking a doctorate, 'is not qualified') with 'a failing grade of 4'

The wasted Summit: he laments the 'utter disregard' of the January 31 Education Summit's recommendations, drafted by 'world-class educators' (Licuanan, Navarro, Echauz, Padolina, Vea, Angeles, Fabella), with Dr. Angeles stressing 'a close linkage between education and the human resources requirements of business' and 'a two-year course after high school' to reach the 12-year standard

The Macapagal model and the appeal: like CJP's Kapampangan father, 'the poor boy from Lubao' Diosdado Macapagal had 'a passion for education' but 'attained his dream' -- valedictorian, bar topnotcher, 'two doctorates' -- 'liberat[ing] himself from destitution through education'; so CJP urges his daughter GMA, with 'two years more,' to 'have a passion for academic excellence,' appoint 'a permanent CHEd chair' and organize 'the Legal Education Board,' giving 'millions of Filipino students an opportunity to fulfill their dreams of conquering ignorance and poverty'

stances.claim: Education is 'the gateway to success and the way out of grinding poverty' -- as CJP's own rise from hawking newspapers to the Court, and Diosdado Macapagal's from Lubao to the presidency, both prove.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument-by-autobiography: grounding a policy claim in lived experience

stances.claim: The government has shown 'sheer neglect of higher education' -- failing the 12-year global standard, leaving CHEd without a qualified permanent chair, and ignoring the Education Summit's recommendations.
stances.rhetorical_move: indictment-by-evidence: stacking concrete failures (PACU, Neri, the Summit)

stances.claim: With two years left, GMA should make education her legacy -- appointing a permanent CHEd chair and organizing the Legal Education Board -- to give 'millions of Filipino students an opportunity' to conquer 'ignorance and poverty.'
stances.rhetorical_move: direct-appeal: addressing the president with a concrete to-do list

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's June 22, 2008 Inquirer column, urges President Arroyo to make education 'one of her enduring legacies,' built on his family's faith that education is 'the gateway to success and the way out of grinding poverty.' His father, who 'did not finish high school,' worked 'doubly hard as a lowly government employee' to send all four children through college (sister Tessie 'summa cum laude,' brother Nardo topping the engineers' board); steering CJP to law but unable to afford UP bus fare, he said 'Diyan ka sa FEU. Hindi na kailangan ang pamasahe' -- advice made 'prophetic' by his early death. CJP kept his FEU scholarship by 'selling bibles to [his] professors and textbooks to [his] classmates,' having 'hawked newspapers, peddled cigarettes, and shined shoes.' Unable to pursue a Yale master's, he 'visited on [his] children [his] frustrated postgraduate aspiration' -- four daughters with graduate degrees from California, Chicago, Michigan and Harvard, a son with 'two masters and a PhD' from Stanford -- and won scholarships for his law clerks. Begging pardon for the 'immodest breast-thumping,' he indicts the government's 'sheer neglect of higher education': the failure to meet 'the 12-year global standard,' the 170-member PACU's call for a qualified permanent CHEd chair (faulting acting chair Romulo Neri with 'a failing grade of 4'), and the 'utter disregard' of the January 31 Education Summit's expert recommendations. Like CJP's father, 'the poor boy from Lubao' Diosdado Macapagal had 'a passion for education' but 'liberated himself from destitution' through it; so CJP appeals to his daughter GMA, with 'two years more,' to 'have a passion for academic excellence,' appoint 'a permanent CHEd chair' and organize 'the Legal Education Board,' giving 'millions of Filipino students an opportunity to fulfill their dreams of conquering ignorance and poverty.'
